title: [Vantage Point] The ASEAN Summit’s billions: Who pays, who gains?
summary: When a government claims an investment victory, it should explain how the country will profit, rather than letting people confuse an American sales receipt with Filipino wealth

blocks.text: Washington’s US$17-billion headline sounds like a massive windfall, yet most of that money comes from pre-existing airplane orders and proposed loans rather than fresh foreign investment. Before celebrating, Filipinos deserve a clear breakdown of what we are actually buying, what we owe, and what stays in our economy now that the summit has ended.
Washington has put a big price tag on President Donald Trump’s Manila visit: over US$17 billion in business deals and strategic investments for American companies.

Before celebrating that number as a Philippine win, we should ask: Who is buying, who is selling, and who eventually pays? When a Philippine company buys from America, it can support US jobs and benefit Filipino travelers. However, buying a product is not the same as foreign money flowing into our economy to build businesses.

President Trump has one priority on his mind: the American people.$17 billion in commercial deals and strategic investments for U.S. companies secured. 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/pkGCaZJX9z— The White House (@WhiteHouse) November 18, 2026

The White House’s November 18 fact sheet covers commercial deals and investment announcements across the region. For our country, it lists an aircraft and engine sale valued by the White House at $12 billion, plus a proposed military loan exceeding $2 billion.
These two items work differently. Adding them together makes a flashy headline, but tells us little about the real income, business growth, or government debt those deals will create locally.

Look at the airplanes first. Philippine Airlines (PAL) said its agreements with Boeing and GE Aerospace were finalized on November 10, days before ASEAN leaders gathered in Manila for the ASEAN Summit.

PAL’s November 15 announcement traced these plans back to the Farnborough International Airshow in July. Boeing confirmed a finalized order for 15 Dreamliners, with the opportunity to buy five more. Simply put, this deal was underway before Trump’s plane landed.

This timeline does not make the order less real. Turning an early plan into a signed contract is a big step, and leaders love showcasing deals during visits. Still, to know what the summit achieved, we must separate existing deals from new ones created at the meeting. Otherwise, the same deal can be recycled and celebrated as a “new” win whenever a foreign leader visits.

We must also examine the plane count. PAL placed a firm order for 15 planes and has the opportunity to buy five more. Investors need to know when deposits and later payments fall due, how PAL will finance them, and when it can decide whether to buy the additional aircraft. A big headline answers none of these questions.

The $12-billion price tag raises questions. Company announcements do not mention that price, explain how much goes to planes versus engines, or show whether the optional planes are included. Thus, we cannot tell from Washington’s headline how much PAL will pay. Nor should we guess by assuming undisclosed discounts. The honest approach is sticking to what companies shared and leaving unknowns open.

Buying new airplanes gives an airline great tools, but the sticker price does not equal money earned by the Philippines. The benefits at home depend on how PAL uses those planes, how many passengers and how much cargo they carry, what jobs they support, and what remains after operating and financing costs.
When a government claims an investment victory, it should explain how the country will profit, rather than letting people confuse an American sales receipt with Filipino wealth.

PAL has a good reason to upgrade. Newer planes can burn less fuel, replace aging jets, and carry more passengers and cargo. Those upgrades can benefit our country even though the planes are built abroad.
But are the revenues these planes generate over their lifetimes cover acquisition, financing, and operating costs? Or did they just make a political summit look good?

PAL’s November 4 results release shows why we must watch those numbers. In the first nine months of 2026, PAL brought in $2.50 billion in revenue, up 4%. However, it posted a $159-million net loss mainly because fuel costs rose by $339.4 million.

PAL generated $247 million in free cash flow during the period and ended September with $879 million in cash and short-term investments, including net proceeds from $350 million in five-year senior unsecured notes.

These numbers show that cash on hand, accounting earnings, and borrowed money are separate things. Investors must weigh future airplane bills against operating cash flow, existing debt payments, and delivery dates.

Fuel savings can improve operating margins, while financing adds to the cost of owning the aircraft. PAL says deliveries are scheduled in the next decade, so investors should assess costs and benefits as they fall due.

Government borrowing needs its own careful look. The White House said both countries would pursue a Foreign Military Financing loan package exceeding $2 billion. Its announcement gave no final loan terms or disbursement details. Any borrowing under the package would carry repayment obligations, with the cost to taxpayers depending on the final terms.

Naturally, a strong military has value beyond profit. Protecting our seas, bridges, and borders keeps the country safe so businesses can grow and people can work. Still, the public deserves basic details before judging affordability: Who borrows the money, what is the interest rate, how many years do we pay it back, and what will maintaining new gear cost? Because defense is vital, we need smart financing so our military can run and repair equipment long after publicity photo opportunities end.
Manila should publish a public register identifying signed contracts, optional purchases, proposed loans, and early promises. It should note earlier announcements and track progress.

Every project should show local spending, Filipino jobs created, debts taken on, and expected benefits. Washington rightly measures success by American sales and jobs. Our government must show what Filipinos gain, what we owe, and whether benefits last after visiting leaders fly home. – Rappler.com
